K E Y W O R D S
brain-computer interfaces, brain-inspired computing, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, large AI models
Large artiﬁci cial intelligence (AI) models, such as DeepSeek
and ChatGPT, are set to revolutionize brain-computer in-
terfaces (BCIs) by enhancing brain signal decoding accuracy
and optimizing user interaction. They employ multimodal
fusion, contextual reasoning, and deep learning to improve
signal processing, reduce noise, and personalize interfaces.
Despite signiﬁca cant progress, challenges such as data privacy,
interpretability, and alignment with biological networks
remain. Overcoming these obstacles will require interdisci-
plinary collaboration to fully unlock the potential of these
technologies in healthcare and beyond.
Over the past two decades, BCIs have enabled human–
computer interaction by decoding neural signals, opening
new
avenues
for
rehabilitating
paralysis
and
treating
neurodegenerative diseases.[1] Meanwhile, brain-inspired
computing
seeks
to
overcome
the
energy
efﬁci ciency
limitations of traditional von Neumann architectures by
simulating biological neural networks, thereby advancing
next-generation AI hardware.[2] However, traditional BCIs
are limited by noise interference and the low throughput of
electroencephalography (EEG) signals, which hinder im-
provements in decoding accuracy.[3] Although brain-inspired
computing has advanced with models like spiking neural
networks (SNNs), challenges remain in efﬁci ciency and
simulation
accuracy.

this
backdrop,
large
AI
models, exempliﬁed ed by DeepSeek, have demonstrated

disruptive potential.[4] Their multimodal fusion, contextual
reasoning, and self-supervised learning capabilities may
revolutionize
brain
signal
decoding,
for
example,
by
enhancing the accuracy of motor intention recognition
through semantic correlation. By leveraging semantic cor-
relation, these models can better interpret latent information
in brain signals, thereby improving motor intention decod-
ing, especially in complex tasks or when signals are
ambiguous, and enabling more precise identiﬁca cation of an
individual's true motor intentions. The deep integration of
large AI models with BCIs and brain-inspired computing is
emerging as a crucial frontier in advancing both brain
science and AI.
Large AI models, with their powerful data processing
capabilities, ability to simulate complex patterns, and advan-
tage
in
integrating
cross-disciplinary
knowledge,
hold
immense potential inboth BCIs andbrain-inspired computing.
First, these models can efﬁci ciently process massive datasets-a
critical advantage in BCIs, where brain signals like EEG and
functional magnetic resonance imaging contain rich, detailed
information. By applying deep learning techniques, large AI
models extract features and uncover latent patterns, thereby
enabling more efﬁci cient human–machine interaction. Second,
these models integrate insights from computer science,
neuroscience, and other ﬁelds to offer innovative solutions for
BCIs. They not only enhance the decoding accuracy of brain
signals but also optimize the overall brain–computer interac-
tion. Speciﬁca cally, large AI models excel in signal decoding
and real-time feedback by efﬁci ciently extracting features from
multimodal brain signals, reducing noise interference through
advanced ﬁltering and signal enhancement algorithms, and
ultimately improving decoding accuracy. Moreover, these
models can personalize interface strategies by leveraging
contextual reasoning to accurately recognize user intentions,
thereby boosting the accuracy of intention recognition. This
adaptability allows BCIs to deliver real-time feedback and
personalized adjustments based on each user's brain signals,
greatly enhancing the overall user experience.
In the ﬁeld of brain-inspired computing, large AI models
offer equally transformative insights. By mimicking the
brain's neural network architecture, these models enhance
both the efﬁci ciency and intelligence of brain-inspired sys-
tems. Their deep neural network structures mirror the con-
nectivity patterns of biological neurons, enabling more
accurate simulations of the brain's information processing
mechanisms. Furthermore, model compression techniques
such as quantization and knowledge distillation not only
improve the efﬁci ciency of brain-inspired computing but also
optimize hardware energy efﬁci ciency, boost computational
performance, and reduce the energy consumption of SNN
hardware. In neural simulation and learning algorithms,
large AI models can replicate the brain's integration
process, from local microcircuits to global functional
networks, through hierarchical representations. Moreover,
optimization
algorithms
derived
from
the
dynamic
parameter updating mechanisms of large models enable
brain-inspired hardware to autonomously reconstruct con-
nections after damage, opening new avenues for simulating
neural plasticity.
However, despite their immense potential, large AI
models still face signiﬁca cant challenges in these ﬁelds. Issues
such as data privacy, model opacity, and limited interpret-
ability persist. For example, in BCI applications, EEG sig-
nals involve sensitive user data, making data security and

protection against information leakage critical priorities. In
addition, the “black-box” nature of these models results in
decision-making processes that lack sufﬁci cient transparency,
which is particularly problematic in high-risk areas such as
healthcare.[5] Furthermore, these models depend on algo-
rithms that are not biologically interpretable, such as back-
propagation, which fundamentally differs from the pulse
timing-dependent characteristics of real neural networks. A
considerable gap remains, especially in addressing the
complexity and adaptability of biological neural networks.
Bridging these gaps and advancing large AI models to
achieve further breakthroughs in BCIs and brain-inspired
computing remains a key focus for future research.
Large AI models have demonstrated potential to drive
rapid advancements in BCIs and brain-inspired computing.
Their efﬁci cient data processing capabilities and deep learning
techniques can enhance brain signal decoding accuracy,
optimize human–computer interaction, and provide effective
computational models for brain-inspired systems. However,
despite signiﬁca cant progress, these models still face a range
of challenges, including technical, ethical, and hardware-
related issues. Key concerns involve data privacy, model
interpretability, and the differences between AI models and
real neural networks, all of which require further resolution
(Figure 1).
In the future, the integration of AI and neuroscience will
be essential for advancing the ﬁeld, particularly in improving
model interpretability and biological simulation. Moreover,
BCI applications are expected to expand, especially in
healthcare, virtual reality, and human–computer interaction.
AI can also reduce hardware requirements, facilitating the
development of portable, compact wearable BCI devices that
enhance accessibility and usability. Achieving these goals
will depend on interdisciplinary collaboration. By fostering
close cooperation among neuroscience, AI, and hardware
engineering, we can drive the development of smarter, more
personalized BCI technologies to address complex global
challenges.
